solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Horrible smell I detected in dry part of prison — one painter required!

indicators.note: something detected in a place is found inside it, so this letter sits within the next piece

parts.note: BO is body odour
TT means teetotal, so dry
taken as written, set between the two parts of the prison wing
a cell is one room of a prison
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A convict notices a foul stench in the alcohol-free wing of a jail, and somebody wants a painter brought in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dry part of prison' reads as one place, but it splits in two (teetotal plus a room), and the I lands between them. Only 'painter' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Sandro Botticelli was the Florentine Renaissance artist who painted The Birth of Venus.

clue.text: Strike-breaker is imprisoned for raising principles

indicators.note: in a down clue raising lifts the letters upwards, reading them bottom to top
something imprisoned is locked inside, so one word goes within the other

parts.note: a scab works during a strike
taken as written

explanation.surface: A worker who crosses a picket line is jailed for raising points of principle.
explanation.walkthrough: A scab is a worker who breaks a strike. In a down clue, 'raising' means the finished string reads upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The basics are the fundamental principles of a subject, its essentials.

clue.text: Plod takes time on old British motorbike

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time
Rudge was a British motorcycle maker until the 1940s

explanation.surface: A policeman, Plod in British slang, spends time aboard a vintage motorcycle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plod' looks like the British slang for the police, but here it is a verb, to walk heavily.
explanation.definitionFit: To plod is to walk slowly and wearily, the same as to trudge.

clue.text: Hip girl supported by most of European city

indicators.note: most of a word is all bar its final letter
in a down clue being supported means having something placed underneath, so the next piece follows

parts.note: fashionable, in
a girl's name
a Pole is a European, and his nationality adjective

explanation.surface: A trendy young woman propped up by most of a continental city's population.
explanation.walkthrough: 'European city' wants to be read together; the definition is just 'city', and European is POLISH cut short. Indianapolis is the capital of Indiana in the USA.
explanation.definitionFit: Indianapolis is a city, the state capital of Indiana and home of the Indy 500 race.

clue.text: Bit of wheat primarily needed to make bread

parts.note: an ear is the grain-bearing head of a cereal plant

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of needed

explanation.surface: Baking advice: a piece of grain is the key ingredient for a loaf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make bread' looks like baking, but bread is slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Bread is slang for money, so to make bread is to get paid for work.

clue.text: Spun out German article two guys penned

indicators.note: to pen is to shut in an enclosure, so the other letters go inside

parts.note: one man's name, the first half of the pen
G is the abbreviation for German
the definite article
a second man's name, closing the pen

explanation.surface: A German newspaper piece that a pair of blokes wrote was padded out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'German article' wants to be a German word such as der or die, but it splits into the abbreviation for German plus the English definite article, held between two men's names.
explanation.definitionFit: Something spun out has been drawn out or prolonged, so made longer.

clue.text: Help Nancy and Jack first

indicators.note: first says the sailor comes at the front, ahead of the other piece

parts.note: a jack is a sailor, and AB is an able seaman
Nancy is a French city, and the French there say et for and

explanation.surface: A plea for help addressed to a pair of people called Nancy and Jack, with Jack getting priority.
explanation.walkthrough: Nancy looks like a woman's name but is the city in north-east France, so its 'and' is French. A jack is a sailor, like the crossword's able seaman.
explanation.definitionFit: To abet is to assist or encourage someone, usually in wrongdoing, as in aiding and abetting.

clue.text: Black treacle ruined jewellery

indicators.note: something ruined is wrecked, so its letters are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Sticky dark syrup has spoiled someone's jewels.
explanation.walkthrough: Treacle is the British name for molasses; black treacle is the dark kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A bracelet is an ornamental band worn around the wrist, a piece of jewellery.

clue.text: Burlesque? Go without an item of underwear

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so one word goes around the other

parts.note: a go is an attempt, a try
a vest, the British word for an undershirt

explanation.surface: A burlesque show: attempting it without wearing any underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like lacking, but here it means outside: TR-A VEST-Y.
explanation.definitionFit: A burlesque is a grotesque parody, and a travesty is likewise a mocking distorted imitation.

clue.text: Mad hired gun starts to draw six-shooter and gets us all of a quiver

indicators.note: something mad is deranged, so the letters that follow are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, so only the first of each is kept

parts.note: the opening letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A deranged gunman reaching for his revolver leaves everyone trembling with fear.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone all of a quiver is trembling violently, which is what shuddering describes.

clue.text: What's meant to be funny about 19s?

definitions.note: 19 down is BANANA; 'bananas' is slang for crazy, and this answer is a synonym

parts.note: a gag is a joke
a is a dictionary abbreviation for about

explanation.surface: A question asking what is supposed to be comical about the answers to 19.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points to BANANA at 19 down; the plural 'bananas' is slang for mad, and so is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are informal adjectives for someone gone crazy or wildly infatuated.

clue.text: Copies some painters might make

indicators.note: what letters might make is a new word formed by arranging them differently

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Imitations that certain artists could produce, like forgeries.
explanation.definitionFit: To impersonate someone is to imitate them, so copies is a synonym in the verb sense.

clue.text: Stiff drink — tin's knocked back by organisation's employee

parts.note: a cog in the machine is a minor worker in a big organisation

indicators.note: something knocked back is sent the other way, so this word runs right to left

parts.note: a can is a tin

explanation.surface: A worker downs a strong drink straight from a can.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocked back' looks like drinking, matching the surface, but it signals a reversal. A cog in the machine is someone with a small role in a big organisation.
explanation.definitionFit: Cognac is a French brandy, a strong spirit of the sort called a stiff drink.

clue.text: Move at speed with hint of mania?

definitions.text: Move at speed with hint of mania?

indicators.note: to move things is to shift them around, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

indicators.note: a hint is just a trace, here only the opening letter of the next word

parts.note: the first letter of mania

explanation.surface: Racing along with a touch of frenzy.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: a stampede is a frantic rush, moving at speed in a mania.
explanation.definitionFit: A stampede is a sudden panicked charge of a herd or crowd, fast and frenzied.

clue.text: King initially made mistake — nearly imprisoned by massive terrorist organisation

indicators.note: being imprisoned means being held inside, so those letters go within the next word

parts.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king
massive means huge; it forms the prison

indicators.note: nearly is almost all, so the last letter is dropped
initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of made
a mistake is an error

explanation.surface: A monarch first made an error, and was almost locked up by a powerful terror group.
explanation.walkthrough: Two pieces sit inside the word for massive, which itself follows the chess king. The terror group is real history, not part of the surface's royal drama.
explanation.definitionFit: The Khmer Rouge was the Cambodian communist movement under Pol Pot, notorious for mass killings.

clue.text: Triumph — revolutionary machine carrying a lady to Thailand

indicators.note: to carry something is to hold it within, so one piece goes inside the other
a revolution turns things over, so the following word's letters are churned

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
Eve is the first woman in Genesis
T is the international vehicle code for Thailand

explanation.surface: A successful outcome: an insurgent's vehicle transporting a woman to Bangkok.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' wants to be CHE (Guevara), but it is the signal to rearrange machine, which takes EVE inside before T is added.
explanation.definitionFit: A triumph is a notable success, and an achievement is something accomplished with effort.

clue.text: Key opening part of court

parts.note: an opening is a gap, a space
the bar is the rail in a courtroom, and the barristers' profession

explanation.surface: An essential first section of a courtroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key opening' reads like 'crucial start', but Key is the definition: a key on a keyboard.
explanation.definitionFit: The long key at the bottom of a keyboard that types a gap between words.

clue.text: Writer dipping bread in booze

indicators.note: dipping something puts it into a liquid, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: to tope is to drink alcohol heavily
a roll is a small loaf of bread

explanation.surface: An author dunking a piece of bread into his drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'booze' looks like a noun, but tope is an old verb meaning to drink heavily, and it wraps the bread.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Trollope was the Victorian novelist of the Barsetshire books.

clue.text: Wasted model left crumpled purses around

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the rearranged letters wrap the other pieces
something crumpled is crushed out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
to model is to pose for an artist
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A drunken fashion model leaves her crushed handbags lying about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wasted' reads as drunk in the surface, but here it means futile or pointless.
explanation.definitionFit: Effort that is wasted serves no end, so it is without purpose.

clue.text: Handkerchief concealing daughter's hand, partly

indicators.note: concealing something hides it away, so that letter vanishes from the word

parts.note: a bandana is a large patterned handkerchief
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A hankie hiding a girl's hand, at least in part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hand' looks like a body part, but a hand is a bunch of bananas, and one fruit is part of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Bananas grow in clusters called hands, so a single fruit is part of a hand.

clue.text: Have words with British judge about term of sentence

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for British

indicators.note: a term is an end point, so only the final letter of the next word is used

parts.note: the last letter of sentence
to judge something is to rate it

explanation.surface: An argument with a UK judge over the length of a prison sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' is read as 'concerning', the judge ruling on the E that precedes RATE. 'term of sentence' looks like a jail term but is just its end letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To have words with someone is an idiom for scolding them, which is what berate means.

clue.text: Perhaps Lassie trains behind Grimethorpe?

parts.note: Lassie, the film dog, is an example of a collie
RY is the abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: Wondering whether the famous dog is out training in the fields behind a Yorkshire village.
explanation.walkthrough: Grimethorpe is a former coal-mining village in South Yorkshire, famous for its colliery brass band; the question mark marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Grimethorpe had a coal mine, so it is an example of a pit with its buildings and workings.

clue.text: Had food with local native

parts.note: a local is a neighbourhood pub, an inn
ate means had food

explanation.surface: Someone ate a meal alongside a person born in the area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'local' and 'native' look like a pair of people, but in British use a local is your nearby pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A native quality is inborn rather than learned, which is what innate means.

clue.text: Book an office

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a Gospel of the New Testament
second meaning: a lavatory; 'offices' is an old British euphemism for the toilets

explanation.walkthrough: Booking an office sounds like reserving a room, but the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gospel of St John is a book of the Bible, and in American slang the word means a toilet.

clue.text: Slip covering one?

parts.note: surface reading: a petticoat, a slip, worn over a part of the body
setter's reading: a slip is a blunder, and the informal word for a blunder is also slang for the breast a slip would cover

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a mistake, and also the very body part a slip as underwear might be covering; the question mark flags the saucy second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A slip is a small error, and this informal British word means a silly mistake.

clue.text: Driving fast? It's the Italian way!

definitions.text: Driving fast? It's the Italian way!

parts.words: Driving fast? It's the Italian way!
parts.note: surface reading: Italians are known for driving at high speed
setter's reading: a literal way, a road in Italy built for fast driving

explanation.walkthrough: The 'way' is not a manner but a road: the Italian name for a motorway.
explanation.definitionFit: An Italian motorway is a high-speed highway, the national equivalent of a British motorway.

clue.text: Oliver looking embarrassed about Bumble's finale

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round the other

parts.note: someone embarrassed goes red in the face

indicators.note: a finale is the ending, so only the last letter is kept

parts.note: the last letter of Bumble

explanation.surface: Little Oliver Twist blushes over the beadle Mr Bumble's final act.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is Dickens, with Bumble the beadle in Oliver Twist, but Oliver is the actor Oliver Reed, who appeared in the film musical Oliver!
explanation.definitionFit: Oliver is the first name of the actor Oliver Reed, so it stands for his surname here.

clue.text: Short French novelist is with guru for preview

indicators.note: something short is cut down, so the name loses its last letter

parts.note: Jules Verne, French author of Around the World in Eighty Days
taken as written
a guru is a wise teacher, a sage

explanation.surface: A French writer of brief stature is with his spiritual teacher for an advance screening.
explanation.definitionFit: A vernissage is a private viewing of an art exhibition before it opens to the public.
